# 11 `geopandas`

GeoPandas is a Python library that extends the `pandas` library by adding support for geospatial data. In this lesson we will introduce the `geopandas` library to work with vector data. We will also make our first map. 

<!-- TODO
## Learning objectives
-->

## About the data

Wild pigs (*Sus scrofa*) are a destructive invasive species in California, causing significant environmental and agricultural damage. Introduced to the region in the 1700s, they have since spread across the state, impacting native ecosystems through habitat destruction, soil disturbance due to their rooting behavior, and competition with native wildlife for food @finzel_wild_2015. This widespread damage has made managing wild pig populations a critical issue for conservation and agricultural communities in California.

![Wild pig in Santa Teresa Park, CA. [Photo by Don DeBold](https://www.flickr.com/photos/ddebold/52936296848)](/book/images/lesson-10/wild_pig.png){width="70%"}

In this lesson we will use simplified point data about wild pig occurrence records in California from the [Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)](https://www.gbif.org). 
GBIF is an international network and data platform that provides open access to biodiversity data from around the world. By aggregating data from multiple sources, including museums, research institutions, and citizen science initiatives like iNaturalist, GBIF enables scientists, policymakers, and the public to explore and analyze species distribution and environmental trends. 

The data we will use today has been simplified from the complete *Sus scrofa* occurrence data accessed through the GBIF website @gbiforg_user_occurrence_2023. 
This data is shared under a [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 (CC BY-NC 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) license: we can use and share it as long as we credit the source and don't use it for commercial purposes.

Each row in the data is one occurrence record. 
The column names were shortened to fit the 10-character limit of shapefile column names:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `gbifID` | Unique identifier of the record in GBIF. The full record is at `https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/` followed by this ID. |
| `species` | Scientific name of the species |
| `state` | State where the record was made |
| `individual` | Number of individuals recorded |
| `day`, `month`, `year` | Date of the record |
| `inst` | Code of the institution that provided the record, for example a museum or a citizen science platform |
| `collection` | Code of the collection within that institution |
| `catalogNum` | Identifier of the record in the institution's catalog |
| `identified` | Person or institution who identified the species |
| `geometry` | Location of the record |

We will also use a shapefile with the boundary of the state of California, which has a single feature: the outline of the state. 
This boundary comes from the US Census Bureau's 2016 TIGER/Line shapefiles @us_census_bureau_tiger_2016 and was converted to a different CRS for this lesson. 
We will use it as a base layer for our maps, to see where the wild pig records are located within California.

Both datasets are in the `gbif_sus_scrofa_california` and `ca_state_boundary` folders of the course's [shared data folder]({{< var shared-data-folder >}}).

## `geopandas`
In this lesson we will introduce the `geopandas` @jordahl_geopandasgeopandas_2020 Python package. `geopandas` extends `pandas` to work with geospatial data. This is the main package we will be working with in the next few lessons.

Let's start by importing the necessary packages and our data:

```{python}
import os
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```


```{python}
fp = os.path.join('data','gbif_sus_scrofa_california','gbif_sus_scrofa_california.shp')
pigs = gpd.read_file(fp)
pigs.head()
```

```{python}
fp = os.path.join('data','ca_state_boundary','ca_state_boundary.shp')
ca_boundary = gpd.read_file(fp)
ca_boundary
```

::: {.callout-caution}
## One shapefile = multiple files
Although the parameter for `geopandas.read_file()` is only the file with `.shp` extension, remember that we need to have at least the `.shx` and `.dbf` files in the same directory as the `.shp` to read in the data. 
:::

## `GeoSeries` and `GeoDataFrame`

The core data structure in GeoPandas is the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`. 
We can think of it as a `pandas.DataFrame` with a dedicated geometry column that can perform spatial operations. 

The **geometry column** in a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` holds the geometry (point, polygon, etc.) of each spatial feature. This geometry column is of type `geopandas.GeoSeries`. Columns in the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` with attributes about the features are `pandas.Series` like in a regular `pandas.DataFrame`. 

![Image adapted from [*Introduction to GeoPandas*](https://geopandas.org/en/stable/getting_started/introduction.html).](/book/images/lesson-10/geodataframe.png){width="70%"}

#### Example

First, notice that the rightmost column of the `pigs` geo-dataframe is a column named `geometry` whose values indicate points:

```{python}
pigs.head(3)
```

As usual, we can check the type of our objects using the `type` Python function:

```{python}
# Check the data type of the pigs dataframe 
print(type(pigs))

# Check the data type of the geometry column
print(type(pigs.geometry))

# Check the data type of the gbifID column
print(type(pigs['gbifID']))
```

The data type of the geometry column is also reflected when we look at the data types of the values in each column:

```{python}
# Check the data type of each column
pigs.dtypes
```

We can also check the type of each element in the geometry column using the `geom_type` attribute of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`:

```{python}
pigs.geom_type
```

This is a `shapely` point. `shapely` is another Python library used to construct and modify points, lines, and polygons. We will talk more about it in the next lessons.
-->

## CRS

Two other important attributes of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` are its coordinate reference system (CRS) and its extent. 

We can think of the **coordinate reference system (CRS)** as the instructions to locate each spatial feature of our data frame on the surface of the Earth. We access the CRS of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` using the `crs` attribute:

<!--TODO: add the other information about CRS as in the in-class notebook and csv to geodf lesson -->
```{python}
# Access the CRS of the GeoDataFrame
pigs.crs
```

The CRS for our data is the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84), represented by the code EPSG:4326. It uses latitude and longitude in degrees to represent places on Earth. This is a very popular CRS: it is used by GPS and Google Earth, and web-based mapping tools like Google Maps and OpenStreetMap store their coordinates in it. We can obtain more information about our CRS by accessing other attributes:

```{python}
# Examine CRS details
print('Ellipsoid: ', pigs.crs.ellipsoid)
print('Datum: ', pigs.crs.datum)
print('Is geographic?: ', pigs.crs.is_geographic)
print('Is projected?: ', pigs.crs.is_projected)
```

## Extent

The **extent** of the geo-dataframe is the bounding box covering *all* the spatial features in our geo-dataframe. This is formed by finding the points that are furthest west, east, south, and north.

![Spatial extent of different vector data. Image adapted from: National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON)](/book/images/lesson-10/spatial-extent-annotated.png){width="80%"}

We access the extent of a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` using the `total_bounds` attribute:

```{python}
# Obtain the geographic extent of the geo-dataframe
pigs.total_bounds
```

These four numbers represent the `minx`, `miny`, `maxx`, `maxy` values for the bounds of the entire geo-dataframe. 
Notice that the $x$ values are longitudes and the $y$ values are latitudes: even though the CRS information above lists latitude first, `geopandas` follows the convention ($x$, $y$) = (longitude, latitude).

::: {.callout-tip}

## `explore()`

To explore our data interactively, we can use the `explore()` method. 
This creates an interactive map where we can zoom in and out, move around, and hover over each feature to see its attributes:

```{python}
pigs.explore()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check-in
Zoom into a few points on the map. Each point is drawn as an exact location.

1. Think about how the location of a wild pig record was obtained: an iNaturalist observation taken with a phone today vs. a museum specimen collected in the 1930s. How exact do you think each location is?
2. What extra information about each point would you want to have to use this data to decide whether to close a trail or not?
:::

<!--
Instructor notes: 877 of 1,046 longitudes have 6 decimals, but 7 have only 1 decimal (~10 km) and 1 has 2 decimals. Those 8 are museum records (SBMNH 1929-1930, SDNHM, UCLA). pigs_recent has at least 3 decimals.
Decimal places are only a rough guide: trailing zeros are dropped, and coordinates can look precise without being so. For example, the "1818" MVZ records have 6 decimals but GBIF lists a coordinate uncertainty of 9,569 m.
iNaturalist can also obscure locations on purpose (not checked for these records).
The full GBIF download has a coordinateUncertaintyInMeters column, which our simplified copy dropped. That's the "extra information" for Q2.
Statewide map: fine. Choosing a trail: not without uncertainty information.
-->

## Data wrangling

GeoPandas is conveniently built on top of `pandas`, so we may use everything we have learned about data selection, wrangling, and modification for a `pandas.DataFrame` to wrangle `geopandas.GeoDataFrame`s.

#### Example

We only want to use recent data for wild pig observations. 
Before selecting the data, let's look at which years it covers.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check-in
Before running the next cell, write down your prediction: when do you expect the earliest wild pig record in our data to be? 
Think about when wild pigs arrived in California and who could have recorded them back then.
:::

```{python}
# Examine pig observations by year
pigs['year'].value_counts().sort_index()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check-in
1. Does the earliest year match your prediction? Do you trust it? 
2. Run `pigs[pigs['year'] == 1818]`. What do these records have in common? How much do you trust the year now, and where could you check it?
:::

<!--
Instructor notes: all 31 "1818" records are MVZ specimens from the same point (Dye Creek Ranch, 13 mi SE Red Bluff, Tehama County), all dated June 20.
On GBIF (e.g. https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/1145709929) the eventDate is the range "1818-06-20/1999-02-04" and the verbatim date is "not recorded": the simplified course copy kept only the start of a placeholder range.
Clues students can use without GBIF: 31 specimens on one day at one spot, about 90 years before the MVZ was founded (1908), and a large gap with no records until 1910.
Pigs were introduced in the 1700s, so 1818 is not impossible on its own: the pattern of the records is what gives it away.
Q2: the gbifID links each row to its GBIF record page (https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/<gbifID>), which shows the original date fields.
-->

In this analysis, we will use data from 2020 onwards. We can use our usual data selection to subset it:

```{python}
# Select data from 2020 onwards
pigs_recent = pigs[pigs['year'] >= 2020]

# Check length of original dataframe
print('Total number of observations: ' , len(pigs))

# Check length of new dataframe
print('Number of observations since 2020: ' , len(pigs_recent))
```

Notice that this selection also leaves out the records without a year, since a missing value is never greater than or equal to 2020.

## Visualizing our data

### `plot()`

Similarly to a `pandas.DataFrame`, a `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` has a `plot()` method that we can call directly to create a quick, static view of our data.
The geospatial information of the `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` will be used to create the axes of the plot.

#### Example

Let's take a quick look at our recent pigs data:

```{python}
pigs_recent.plot()
```

### Using `matplotlib`

Going forward, we will make more complex visualizations where we add different layers to a map and customize it. 
To do this, we will use `matplotlib` via its `pyplot` interface for creating visualizations. You can review the `matplotlib` basics in this [previous lesson](/book/chapters/lesson-18-linear-regression/lesson-18-linear-regression.qmd).

#### Example

When using matplotlib, it can be useful to think of creating a plot as adding layers to an axes. In this case, the first layer that we want to add to our axes is the `pigs_recent` point data. 
We can plot our data using `matplotlib` like this:

```{python}
# Initialize empty figure and axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Add pigs point plot to our figure's axes
pigs_recent.plot(ax=ax)

# Display figure
plt.show()
```

Then some simple customization for our pigs data could look like this:

```{python}
# Initialize empty figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Add data to axes
pigs_recent.plot(ax=ax,         # Add plot to axes
                 alpha=0.5,     # Adjust transparency
                 color='brown'  # Update point color
                 )

# Update axes 
ax.set_title('Reported "Sus scrofa" sightings in CA (2020-2023)')
ax.set_xlabel('Longitude')
ax.set_ylabel('Latitude')

# Display figure
plt.show()
```
